title: Port Alder Rising Again
premise: Jonah Galloway, a widowed single parent keeping Port Alder's last bookshop afloat, agrees to a fake date with bakery owner Marisol Vega to survive his mother's reunion — but the pretense turns real by dessert. As her bakery lease nears expiration and a developer's offer threatens both their businesses, Jonah must choose between the lucrative publishing career that saved him from debt and the woman who finally sees him clearly. He chooses truth over security, and together they save the harbor block, ending with the bookshop and bakery sharing one rebuilt storefront.
about_author: Ines Halloran is a former small-town bookseller who writes love stories set in coastal towns where everyone knows your business. She lives in Oregon with her family and an opinionated cat named Chapter.

chapters.title: The Reunion Clause
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Cornered by his mother's ultimatum about bringing a date to the Galloway reunion, Jonah panics in the bakery line and blurts an invitation to Marisol, a stranger he's admired for months. The beat: desperate improvisation masking loneliness.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She counters with terms: he'll help fight her lease expiration by rallying the town. They shake on it, both pretending their hearts aren't involved. The beat: wary hope disguised as business.

chapters.title: Rehearsal Dinner
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Their first 'practice date' at the dockside diner goes sideways when his daughter Poppy crashes it and adores Marisol instantly. The beat: terror that real feeling is leaking through the fiction.

chapters.title: Dessert Was the Tell
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. At the reunion itself, a slow dance under string lights dissolves the act; they kiss for real as his family watches. The beat: the fake arrangement collapses into genuine want.

chapters.title: Morning After the Act
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Giddy but frightened, Jonah pulls back, citing Poppy and his fragile finances. Marisol leaves before coffee. The beat: self-protection mistaken for responsibility.

chapters.title: Lease on Life
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Her landlord reveals the harbor block has been sold to developer Corliss Group; her lease ends in ninety days. The beat: dread sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. His old publisher dangles a lucrative editorial job in the city — the money that would erase his debts — contingent on relocating within two months. The beat: temptation wearing the mask of rescue.

chapters.title: Petition Signatures
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The pair canvasses Port Alder for signatures to landmark the harbor block, growing closer through shared purpose. The beat: partnership deepening into intimacy neither names.

chapters.title: Poppy's Question
chapters.summary: Poppy's POV (childlike third). Poppy asks Marisol if she'll stay forever, forcing both adults to confront what they're building. The beat: innocence exposing adult evasion.

chapters.title: Memory of Salt
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Sorting his late wife's belongings, Jonah finds letters revealing she'd planned to leave Port Alder — shattering his shrine to the past. The beat: grief rewritten, memory released.

chapters.title: Corliss Comes Calling
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The developer offers Marisol a sweetened deal: keep her bakery inside a luxury complex if she withdraws from the landmark fight. The beat: survival versus solidarity.

chapters.title: The Secret Ledger
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, guilt-ridden. She secretly considers the offer, hiding it from Jonah while he plans their future storefront. The beat: loyalty cracking under financial fear.

chapters.title: City Interview
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the city, the publisher wows him; an old colleague mentions Corliss Group is the publisher's new majority investor. The beat: the two threats revealed as one.

chapters.title: Overheard at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She learns Jonah interviewed for the job that would fund the developer's project — believing he'd sell out the block she's fighting for. The beat: betrayal misread, trust inverted.

chapters.title: Cold Counter
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A bitter public argument at the town meeting splits them; each accuses the other of choosing money. The beat: pride weaponized, hearts bruised.

chapters.title: Poppy Picks Sides
chapters.summary: Poppy's POV. Poppy refuses to speak to Jonah after Marisol stops coming around, holding up a drawing of the three of them. The beat: a child's clarity cutting through adult stubbornness.

chapters.title: The Letter He Never Sent
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Rereading his wife's letters, Jonah realizes she urged him to choose living over safety. He declines the job and drafts a public letter defending the harbor block. The beat: courage born of memory.

chapters.title: Flour and Forgiveness
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Jonah shows up mid-bake, flour-dusted and honest, explaining everything; Marisol admits she nearly signed Corliss's deal. Mutual confession. The beat: truth as the only foundation worth building on.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the council vote, testimony from townsfolk — led by Poppy presenting the petition — sways the outcome; the block is landmarked. The beat: community as climax, triumph earned collectively.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Turning down the city salary means lean years ahead; Jonah and Marisol plan a shared storefront to halve expenses. The beat: choosing love with eyes open to its price.

chapters.title: Rising Again
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Construction begins on the combined bookshop-bakery; Marisol bakes bread in the old oven her grandmother used. The beat: renewal rooted in heritage rather than escape.

chapters.title: Second Chances, Better Timing
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. One year later, at the reopened shop's first story hour, Jonah proposes with a bookmark instead of a ring; Poppy cheers. The beat: quiet joy — timing finally right because they chose it.
